questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a two-part pattern captures from a longer string
questions.learningObjective: determine which characters a pattern captures and which it leaves behind
questions.stem: READ THIS AND REPORT THE TWO CAPTURED VALUES. DEFINE firstPair(text) { m <- THE FIRST MATCH OF /(\d+)-(\d+)/ IN text ; RETURN GROUP 1 OF m AND GROUP 2 OF m }. DISPLAY firstPair("12-34-56").

options.text: 12 and 34, because a match is taken at the earliest position where the pattern fits and the first group stops at the first separator it meets
34 and 56, because a pattern holding more than one group is read from the right-hand end of the text backwards
options.misconception: believes a multi-group pattern is read right to left

options.text: 12 and 34, because the two groups together must cover the whole text before the match counts as a match at all
options.misconception: believes a match must span the entire text

options.text: 12-34 and 56, because the separator joins the two groups into the first one rather than ending it
options.misconception: believes a separator is captured by the group before it

questions.explanation: The match is sought from the earliest position, so the first digits found are 12, and the first group takes as many digits as it can before the separator stops it, giving 34 for the second group. The trailing 56 is simply left outside the match, because a pattern asks for a piece of text and not for a verdict on the whole. Confirming this by running it gave 12 and 34, which also shows the general rule: a match can start and stop anywhere, and a pattern that must describe the entire text needs anchors at both ends.
questions.hint: Ask where the earliest possible match begins, and where the first group is forced to stop.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A scan that collects every run it finds
questions.learningObjective: trace a repeated scan and report the text it assembles
questions.stem: READ THIS AND REPORT WHAT IT DISPLAYS. DEFINE digitsOf(text) { out <- AN EMPTY LIST ; WHILE A MATCH OF /\d+/ REMAINS IN text { APPEND THE MATCHED TEXT TO out ; RETURN out } DEFINE report(text) { RETURN JOIN(digitsOf(text), "|") }. DISPLAY report("A1B22C333").

options.text: 1|22|333, because the scan resumes after each match, so every run of digits is taken once and the pieces keep the order they were found in
1|2|2|3|3|3, because a run of digits is captured one character at a time rather than as a whole run
options.misconception: believes a repeated-digit quantifier captures single characters

options.text: 1|22|333|12, because the closing run of digits is reported a second time as the scan finishes the text
options.misconception: believes the last match is always collected twice

options.text: 333|22|1, because each new match is placed at the front of the list before the pieces are joined together
options.misconception: believes a collected match list is reversed before it is joined

questions.explanation: The pattern asks for one or more digits, so it takes the whole run at each stop rather than one digit, and a repeated scan resumes where the last match finished, which is what keeps the runs from being found twice. Running it gave 1, 22, then 333, in that order. The rule that does the work here is the resume position: a scan that restarted from the beginning would report the first run over and over, and one that resumed at the character after the run would slice the next match in half.
questions.hint: Ask how many digits one match takes, and where the scan looks next.

then BOLD, because the reluctant quantifier is the one that reaches as far as possible across the text
options.misconception: believes the reluctant quantifier takes the longest possible match

options.text: BOLD then BOLD, because the two quantifiers differ only in how much time they take and not in what they return
options.misconception: believes the two quantifiers agree on the matched text

options.text: B then BOLD, because the angle brackets sit outside the group the quantifier applies to and so are never captured

options.text: TRUE and then TRUE, because the anchors already pin the pattern to exactly eight characters and so leave nothing for a wildcard to absorb

FALSE and then FALSE, because an anchor always governs every part of the pattern however the parts are divided
options.misconception: believes anchors reach across a top-level alternation

options.text: TRUE and then TRUE, because a space is an ordinary character that neither half of the pattern needs to forbid
options.misconception: believes grouping an alternation changes nothing about which values pass

options.text: FALSE and then TRUE, because writing the alternatives inside brackets turns a test that fails into one that passes
options.misconception: believes brackets make a check looser rather than scoping it

questions.explanation: An alternation is the lowest-binding operator, so a bar with nothing around it divides the whole pattern into two independent patterns, and the anchors are carried along by whichever half they were written next to. TRUE and then TRUE, because the end anchor is only examined once the whole pattern has matched from end to end
options.misconception: believes the end anchor is checked only at the very end

options.text: FALSE and then FALSE, because a text holding two separators can never satisfy a pattern that names one of them
options.misconception: believes a second separator is by itself enough to fail a match

options.text: TRUE and then FALSE, because the greedy first group swallows the first separator and leaves nothing for the pattern to match
options.misconception: believes a digit group can capture a separator character

The routine finishes after two passes, because the digits are taken in one run and the position then steps past the end of the text
options.misconception: believes a zero-digit pattern still consumes the digits it meets

options.text: The routine finishes after four passes, because each pass advances the position by exactly one character regardless of the match
options.misconception: believes the step size is independent of the match length

options.text: The routine reports no match at all, because a pattern that can match nothing never matches anything anywhere
options.misconception: believes an optional pattern always fails

options.text: FALSE and then TRUE, because a word boundary requires that the letters are not flanked by other word characters, and the same letters inside a longer word are flanked
TRUE and then TRUE, because a word boundary is satisfied wherever the letters of the word appear at all
options.misconception: believes a boundary test is satisfied by letters inside a word

options.text: FALSE and then FALSE, because a pattern is never found inside a longer word under any form
options.misconception: believes a search cannot look inside a word at all

options.text: TRUE and then FALSE, because a word boundary matches more freely than the bare pattern that carries none
options.misconception: believes a boundary loosens a search rather than narrowing it

questions.explanation: A word boundary is a claim about the neighbours, not about the letters themselves: it holds where a word character meets a non-word character or the edge of the text. Inside CONCATENATE the letters cat are followed by another letter, so the trailing boundary cannot hold and the whole-word test says no, while the bare pattern never asked about neighbours and says yes. Running both gave FALSE and then TRUE, and the practical consequence is that a search over a name list will report catalogue as a hit on cat unless the boundary is asked for on both sides.
questions.hint: Ask what stands either side of the letters where the match is claimed.

TRUE and then TRUE, because a counted group already stands for a letter in either case at once
options.misconception: believes a repeated letter group covers both cases by itself

options.text: FALSE and then FALSE, because ignoring case can only matter for patterns that name no letters at all
options.misconception: believes ignoring case has no effect on a named letter

options.text: TRUE and then FALSE, because ignoring case narrows a pattern down to a single case instead of widening it
options.misconception: believes case-insensitivity restricts rather than widens

DEFINE normalise(text) { lines <- SPLIT(text, THE LINE FEED CHARACTER) ; FOR EACH line IN lines { REPLACE(line, ITS TRAILING CARRIAGE RETURN, NOTHING) } ; RETURN lines }. DEFINE joinLines(lines) { RETURN JOIN(lines, THE LINE FEED CHARACTER) }. DISPLAY LENGTH(joinLines(normalise("ALPHA\r\nBETA\r\nGAMMA"))).

18, because normalising the line endings changes the characters without changing how many there are

options.misconception: believes the two halves of a line break are removed together

options.text: 17, because the carriage return after the last line is kept since no line break follows it
options.misconception: believes a trailing carriage return belongs to the final line

options.misconception: believes a count is independent of how the scan resumes

options.text: 1 and then 1, because the same text and the same piece always produce the same count however the counting is written
options.misconception: believes two counting routines cannot disagree

questions.learningObjective: predict the effect of running a replacement over its own output
questions.stem: READ THIS AND REPORT WHAT IT DISPLAYS. DEFINE tidy(s) { REPLACE(s, EVERY PAIR OF ADJACENT a's, ONE a) ; RETURN s }. DISPLAY tidy("AAAA") AND DISPLAY tidy(tidy("AAAA")).

options.text: AA and then A, because the first pass leaves a pair of adjacent letters behind, so a second pass over the same text finds work to do and the routine is not safe to run twice

options.text: AA and then AA, because a replacement is applied only to the text handed in, never to what a previous pass produced
options.misconception: believes a second pass ignores the first pass's output

options.text: A and then AA, because each pass shortens the run by one letter and the two values are therefore the wrong way round
options.misconception: believes repeating a cleanup makes the text longer

questions.explanation: One pass over four adjacent letters takes the first pair and the second pair, because those are the two pairs it finds, and the two single letters it leaves are themselves adjacent, which is the whole difficulty. The output is therefore still a pair, and a second pass shortens it again to a single letter. options.text: 2026/09-26 and then 2026/09-26, because a pattern cannot be told to change one hit rather than all of them

questions.topic: A pattern that describes a language rather than one text
questions.learningObjective: explain why a pattern accepts any text containing a described piece
questions.stem: A checker applies a pattern to a whole submitted value and reports a match if the pattern is found anywhere inside it. What set of values does such a checker accept?

options.text: Every value that contains the described piece somewhere, at any position and with any amount of text before and after it, because a match is a piece of a text and not a description of the whole
Only the values that are exactly the described piece, because a pattern always describes an entire value and never part of one
options.misconception: believes a match must span the whole value

options.text: The values that begin with the described piece, because a search always starts at the first character of a value

questions.topic: Why a short pattern can cost far more work than it looks
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes a pattern take many attempts on a long text
questions.stem: A four-character pattern is checked against a text of forty thousand characters and takes far longer than four times forty thousand character tests would suggest. What accounts for the extra work?

options.text: An unbounded group takes as much as it can and then gives characters back one at a time when a later part of the pattern fails, and a text with many nearly-matching stretches multiplies those attempts at every starting place

options.misconception: believes matching compares every character of a text with every character of a pattern

options.text: The pattern is compiled once per character of the text, and compilation is the expensive part of the work
options.misconception: believes the cost is in preparing the pattern repeatedly

options.text: Because the split only reports what lay between the delimiters, and between two delimiters with nothing in between there is a piece of length zero in both cases, so the record has to carry some other sign that the field was omitted
Because a split always discards empty pieces, so a blank value and an absent one both vanish and leave the same shortened list
options.misconception: believes a split removes empty pieces from its result

options.text: Because an empty piece is returned as a null marker rather than as text, and a null marker cannot be compared with anything
options.misconception: believes an empty piece arrives as a null marker

options.text: Because the two cases differ only in the delimiter used, so reading with the wrong separator is what makes them look alike
options.misconception: believes the confusion is caused by the choice of separator

questions.explanation: A blank value and an omitted value are two different facts about the record, and the line as written encodes only one of them, because in both cases the characters between the delimiters are simply absent. options.text: Nothing needs fixing, because a value that contains the separator is malformed and the routine that wrote it is at fault for writing it

options.misconception: believes the uniqueness check is the forgiving one to make

options.text: Nothing is needed, because a value already sitting inside a larger text is not itself re-read, so nothing can be confused with syntax
options.misconception: believes an embedded value is never read back

options.text: Nothing needs to be true, because a replacement run over text it has already produced is by definition the same operation and so the same result

options.misconception: believes the threshold has no independent meaning

options.text: Because a similarity figure can always be raised by asking for it more than once, so the threshold is what stops the matcher from doing that
options.misconception: believes repeated scoring can inflate a figure

options.misconception: believes a zero score means the sequences match

options.text: It has settled nothing at all, because a score computed without knowing the scoring rule cannot be interpreted by anyone reading the result
options.misconception: believes a score is uninterpretable without the rule

options.text: It has settled that the two sequences differ in every position, because one point for agreeing and minus one for differing can only cancel if nothing agrees
options.misconception: believes cancellation requires zero agreements

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a pattern that can match nothing is unsafe inside a scan
questions.learningObjective: argue that a zero-length match removes the only thing a scanning loop uses to make progress
questions.stem: A scanning routine advances its position by the length of each match, and it is handed a pattern that can match an empty piece. Explain, in a short paragraph, why this can never finish.

answer.exemplar: The loop's only evidence of progress is the length of the match, because nothing else in it changes between one pass and the next: the text is fixed and the position is the only variable. A pattern written with zero or more of something is allowed to report that it found none of them, and that is a legitimate answer rather than a failure, so the length handed back is zero. Adding zero leaves the position exactly where it was, the condition at the top of the loop is therefore still true, and the routine returns to the same character with the same pattern and the same result. Nothing about the second pass differs from the first, so no number of passes will change anything, which is why the process appears to hang rather than to fail. The fix is to make progress unconditional: either write the pattern so that it must consume at least one character, or keep the rule that an empty match still advances the position by one, so that even the degenerate case moves the scan forward.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names the position as the loop's only source of progress, says that a zero-length match is a legitimate result rather than a failure, and concludes that the second pass is identical to the first so no number of passes can help. An answer that only says the pattern matches nothing stops one step short, because it does not explain why matching nothing does not eventually end the loop. The best answers also give the two repairs and say which condition each restores, since a fix that does not restore unconditional progress leaves the same hang waiting for the next text that happens to begin with a non-matching character.
questions.hint: Ask what the loop changes between one pass and the next.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why removing every pair is not the same as removing every letter
questions.learningObjective: argue that a repeated replacement is not safe to run twice unless nothing of what it matched survives
questions.stem: A cleanup replaces every pair of adjacent letters with a single letter, and the same record processed twice comes out two different lengths. Explain, in a short paragraph, what the cleanup is failing to notice about its own result.

answer.exemplar: The cleanup is checking only for the pattern it was written to find and not checking whether its own output still contains that pattern. Replacing the pairs in a run of four letters finds two pairs and rewrites them, but the two single letters it leaves are themselves adjacent, so the text it has just produced is once again a match for the very rule it applied. A second pass therefore finds work to do and shortens the text again, which is why running the cleanup twice on four letters gives two letters and then one. The routine is not repeatable in the sense that matters, because repeating it changes the answer, and a cleanup that is run again by a retry or by a later migration cannot be trusted to leave the data where the first run put it. The property to insist on is that the output contains no further occurrence of the pattern, and the way to get it is to write the pattern so that it matches a whole run of the letter at once rather than a pair, which finishes the job in one pass and leaves nothing for a second.

questions.explanation: A strong answer says the output still contains the pattern the routine was looking for, gives the run of four letters turning into two and then one as the demonstration, and connects that to the reason a second pass differs from the first. An answer that only says the pattern is not greedy enough identifies the weakness but stops short of the consequence, which is that the cleanup cannot be run again safely and so cannot be part of a pipeline that might run twice. The strongest answers finish by naming the property to insist on, that the output holds no further copy of the pattern, and by pointing at the one change that establishes it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the text the routine produced still contains what it was searching for.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a fuzzy match is being asked to trade away
questions.learningObjective: argue that a similarity threshold trades missed matches against false matches and cannot avoid both
questions.stem: A system matches typed names against stored names using a similarity figure and a cutoff. Explain, in a short paragraph, why raising the cutoff improves one kind of error and worsens another.

answer.exemplar: The cutoff is the boundary of the set of pairs the system is willing to call the same, and moving that boundary can only push pairs out of the set, never into it. So raising it necessarily removes the loose pairs that were being accepted by mistake, which is the improvement: a name that shares little with the typed value stops being reported as a hit. The same movement also removes the near misses, such as a six-letter stored name differing from what was typed by one letter, which scores 83.3 and is inside a cutoff of 80 but outside one of 90, and those are exactly the pairs a person would have wanted joined. Lowering the cutoff reverses both effects at once, trading a fresh supply of false matches for a fresh supply of correct ones. This is why one number cannot be tuned until both errors disappear, because the two move in opposite directions together, and a system that must drive one of them to nothing needs a second source of information, such as the postcode or the date of birth, rather than a stricter line.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names the two kinds of error as accepting a pair that should have been refused and refusing a pair that should have been accepted, and ties each to the direction the cutoff moves. Raising the cutoff shrinks the set of pairs that can be accepted, so it necessarily removes the loose pairs that were wrongly accepted before, and it also removes the near misses that a person would have recognised as the same name, and the second removal is the cost. A cut of 80 percent accepts a spelling with one letter changed in a six-letter name while still letting through pairs that share little, and a cut of 90 percent refuses the same spelling, so the choice is not a tuning matter but a statement of what the system is for. The best answers finish by noting that the two errors cannot both be driven down by moving one number, and that a system that must avoid one of them at all costs needs a second source of information rather than a stricter cut.
questions.hint: Ask which pairs stop being accepted when the cutoff rises, and which pairs were being accepted before.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What counts as the same text when two copies are compared
questions.learningObjective: argue that normalising before comparing is a decision about meaning and not only about tidiness
questions.stem: A change-detection check reports two copies of one document as different, and a colleague proposes normalising line endings before comparing them. Explain, in a short paragraph, why that proposal settles a question about meaning and not merely about tidiness.

answer.exemplar: Deciding to normalise is deciding what counts as the same document, and that decision has consequences beyond making the comparison tidy. If the two-character line break is treated as a variation with no meaning, then the two copies are equal and the check reports no change, which is what the colleague wants. But a tool that writes one-character breaks and a tool that writes two-character breaks produce texts that differ in nothing a reader of the document would ever notice, and a check that treats them as different is reporting a fact about the tools rather than about the document. The risk runs the other way too: somewhere a stray carriage return can itself be the thing that matters, a value whose trailing whitespace is significant, a file that has been padded, and in those places the same normalisation hides a real difference rather than a phantom one. The honest form of the proposal is therefore to state the rule, apply it to both copies, and keep the strict comparison available for the cases where the difference is the point, so the decision is visible to whoever reads the result instead of being buried in the checker.

questions.explanation: A strong answer says that deciding to normalise is deciding what counts as the same document, explains that the difference being removed is one no reader would notice, and then gives the other side, that a difference in line endings is sometimes the very thing under investigation. An answer that only argues the two copies are effectively the same stops one step short, because it treats normalisation as obviously right rather than as a choice with a stated rule. The best answers also say how to make the choice safe, which is to name the rule, apply it to both sides, and keep the strict comparison available where the difference matters, so the decision is legible to a reader instead of hidden in the check.
questions.hint: Ask whether the characters being removed could ever be the thing someone is looking for.

questions.topic: Pairing a shape check with the rule it still cannot express
questions.learningObjective: pair a pattern-based check with the follow-up rule it leaves to somebody else
questions.stem: A form checks a submitted date first with a pattern and then with a second rule. Which option pairs the pattern with the check that actually finishes the job?

options.text: Pattern: two digits, a hyphen, two digits, a hyphen, four digits, and nothing else. Second check: read the three numbers and confirm the month is one of the twelve, the day is within that month, and the year is inside the range the form allows
Pattern: two digits, a hyphen, two digits, a hyphen, four digits, and nothing else. Second check: run the same pattern once more, because a value that passes twice is a value that is certainly right
options.misconception: believes repeating a shape check strengthens it

options.text: Pattern: any eight digits with a hyphen anywhere among them. Second check: refuse any value whose year is earlier than the current one, because a date in the past is the only value a form cannot accept
options.misconception: believes the only rule worth adding concerns the year

options.text: Pattern: the shape as written. Second check: convert the value to a date and let the conversion decide, because a value that cannot be converted cannot be a real date
options.misconception: believes a conversion applies the calendar rule by itself

questions.explanation: The pattern is responsible for shape and the second check is responsible for range, and the pairing works only when each does the half it is able to do. A pattern can say two digits followed by a hyphen, and it cannot say that the number it just matched is one of the twelve months, because that is a statement about the value of a piece rather than about its shape. The pairing in the second option adds nothing because a pattern is not a coin, and the pairing in the fourth relies on a conversion that will quietly apply some arbitrary rule to a value like 45-13-2026 rather than refuse it.
questions.hint: Ask which half of validity a pattern can express, and which half it cannot.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Pairing a count that runs high with the two rules that would fix it
questions.learningObjective: pair an inflated count of a word with the two search rules responsible
questions.stem: A report says the word CAT appears eleven times in a body of text, and a careful reader counts six. Which option pairs the two rules the search must be holding wrong?

options.text: It is comparing without regard to case, so differently cased spellings are counted, and it is asking for the letters anywhere rather than as a whole word, so a longer name is counted as well; the fix is to make the comparison case-sensitive and to require a word boundary on both sides
It is scanning from the end of the text and counting backwards, and it is adding one for the first match; the fix is to scan forwards and to start the count at one
options.misconception: believes the direction of the scan changes the count

options.text: It is comparing without regard to case, and it is resuming after every starting place rather than after each match; the fix is to make the comparison case-sensitive and to resume past each whole match
options.misconception: believes testing every starting place is what finds extra words

options.text: It is asking for the letters anywhere rather than as a whole word, and it is counting the letters of the word as well as the word; the fix is to require a word boundary and to count the match rather than its length
options.misconception: believes a count of a word should include its letters

questions.explanation: A count five higher than a careful count has to come from a rule that is admitting things it should not, and the two rules that admit extra hits are the case-blind comparison and the absence of a word boundary, which is why they are the pair named here. The count does not depend on the direction a text is read in, and resuming after every starting place changes which occurrences are seen but not the number of words a reader would count, so the third option is ruled out. The honest fix is to state both rules in the report, because a figure of eleven is not wrong by itself, it is wrong with respect to a rule the reader has not been told.
questions.hint: Ask which two rules would let a search report a word that the text does not hold as a word.
